sources.title: Welcome and introductory talks (opening session)
sources.limitations: Minutes derived from an automatic transcript of the opening session. They do not separate the welcome and the two introductory talks, so statements are not attributed to individual speakers. Numerical values are not used.

sources.title: Global Data & Global Patterns
sources.limitations: Minutes derived from an automatic transcript of a review-and-recommendation keynote; no substantive question-and-answer exchange was recorded.

src-welcome.note: The minutes cover the opening session without separating its speakers; whether they cover both introductory talks, and where the clip sits in the session, is not established.

claim.text: The closing record listed MJO initiation, propagation and weakening through the Maritime Continent, and the relationship between the eastward-propagating MJO and other intraseasonal modes, as aspects existing theories do not comprehensively explain, and urged more theoretical attention to northward-propagating boreal-summer intraseasonal oscillations.
The theory keynote cautioned that isolating the MJO as a single large-scale mode can miss its interactions with convectively coupled synoptic waves and mesoscale convective systems.
The theory keynote described multicloud frameworks in which shallow clouds, congestus, deep and stratiform clouds and low-level moisture convergence take part in wave selection and organization.

The modeling keynote noted many examples in which moisture-sensitive convection schemes or low-level moistening by shallow convection strengthen the simulated MJO, while intercomparisons still call for process-level explanation rather than tuning alone.

The Global Data & Global Patterns keynote argued that convective parameterizations have represented heating more fully than the momentum transport and dynamical organization of mesoscale convective systems, that kilometre-scale grids do not resolve organization automatically, and that interactions from mesoscale systems to the MJO, westerly wind bursts and El Niño, including downward QBO influence on mesoscale systems, should be treated as one continuum.

A final-day group report distinguished uses of AI for operational forecasting and services (accuracy, reliability, usability), for scientific research (physical processes and sources of predictability) and for AI-model development (diagnostics and training strategies).

The closing record named whether improvements in forecast skill also represent improvements in physical understanding as a central question, treating them as related but distinct goals, and asked whether summary skill metrics can show that an AI model gets the right answer for the right reasons.

The final-day minutes' own summary table describes the physical explainability of AI as an active disagreement—views differed on how much understanding is necessary and for whom—and lists regional impact evaluation and co-design with users as areas of broad convergence. These are labels in the minutes, not formal resolutions.

Asked what evidence from AI could convince researchers who hold different physical hypotheses, the closing discussion answered that explanations should be tested against observations rather than treated as matters of belief, and reaffirmed direct observations as a constraint on both models and theories.

The Global Data & Global Patterns keynote recommended representing organization and momentum transport explicitly in convective parameterizations and evaluating them in uncoupled and ocean-coupled models against Maritime Continent passage, tropical variability spectra, twin cyclones, El Niño onset and QBO relations, not MJO amplitude alone.

The opening session recommended studying the MJO as a system that includes convective organization, the ocean, equatorial waves and the mid-latitude circulation, and testing deficiencies in vertical resolution, ocean coupling, momentum transport and cold pools individually rather than treating higher resolution alone as the solution.

The theory plenary reported that long-term West Pacific observations are underused because older data take time and funding to process and are not widely known; the usage figures quoted were the speaker's estimates, not verified statistics.

The applications keynote noted that gains in MJO index skill need not raise regional impact skill by the same amount, and that MJO-conditioned skill gains appear for tropical rainfall in several studies but are mixed in the extratropics, varying with region, season, metric and study, with limited samples and ENSO or QBO background states affecting interpretation.

The opening session described a period in which model-physics changes at an operational centre improved both the simulated MJO amplitude and the prediction of related North Atlantic teleconnections, but also reported that mid-latitude circulation responses following the MJO remain weaker than observed in recent reforecasts, possibly because the signal is lost amid other variability in operational systems.
Rushley framed the talk around the point that MJO index skill and the skill of extratropical circulation and impact forecasts are not the same.

Final-day group reports stated that improving forecast scores is not equivalent to creating societal value, that the same MJO phase need not produce the same impacts everywhere, and that the user-facing question is how a predicted state alters a risk at a given location; users differ in the variables, lead times and uncertainty information they need.

The closing record questioned deterministic headline thresholds such as an RMM correlation of 0.5, encouraged probabilistic and state-dependent verification, and noted that the same rainfall can have different consequences depending on antecedent soil moisture, river discharge and terrain.

A final-day plenary contribution proposed coordinated phenomenon-tracking and multiscale diagnostics for the MJO together with equatorial waves, tropical cyclones, monsoon variability and ENSO, suggesting that better AI skill might reflect better representation of interacting variability rather than of the MJO alone.

synthesis.overarching_question: What prevents the community from turning increasingly realistic MJO representations into reliable physical understanding and useful regional prediction?

executive.text: Read across the records, the workshop's contributions can be connected by one question: what prevents increasingly realistic representations of the MJO from becoming reliable physical understanding and useful regional prediction? The records point to gaps at each link rather than to a single obstacle. Field observations document progressive moistening and boundary-layer processes, but at few sites, and reanalysis comparisons are not independent of the soundings assimilated into them. Theory offers several mechanisms that reproduce similar large-scale signals without an agreed test to discriminate among them, and lifecycle transitions such as initiation and termination lack operational definitions. Dynamical and AI forecast systems can reach competitive index skill, yet weakening over the Maritime Continent and the representation of organized convection remain poorly constrained, and index skill alone does not show which processes are right. In applications, similar MJO skill can coexist with different regional skill, because heating location, propagation speed, background flow, ENSO and local exposure intervene before a forecast informs a decision. These connections are the author's reading across separate talks and discussions, not a framework the workshop adopted; the strands were discussed largely in different sessions, and several were recorded only in part.

insights.title: No single MJO theory is agreed, and reproducing MJO structure does not by itself identify a mechanism
insights.text: The theory keynote reviewed mechanisms that can produce similar large-scale signals while differing in circulation structure and parameter dependence. The closing record kept three views side by side—a unified account, theoretical pluralism, and making each theory's predictions and assumptions testable—without choosing among them. The sharpest recorded dispute was methodological: whether diagnostics that separate better- from worse-performing models identify a mechanism, or whether process interventions and observational tests of a theory's assumptions are needed first. The recurring direction is testability, not a winning theory.
insights.reason: Both Phase 8 insights rested on Q01 and largely the same records. The first title foregrounded one of three views recorded side by side in the closing discussion.

insights.title: Initiation, propagation and termination need operational definitions
insights.text: The theory discussion found no shared conceptual account or operational definition of initiation: how synoptic disturbances, organized convection and the growth of an MJO envelope combine remains unclear, and real onset may be finite-amplitude and stochastic rather than infinitesimal growth. A breakout asked for objective criteria to tell weakening, stalled propagation and termination apart, and the closing record listed initiation and Maritime Continent weakening among aspects existing theories do not explain. No accepted criterion was established.
insights.reason: The breakout asked for criteria to distinguish weakening, stalling and termination; Phase 8 wording said it distinguished them.

insights.title: Several contributions treat the MJO as part of multiscale interactions rather than as an isolated mode
insights.text: The theory keynote cautioned that isolating the MJO as a single large-scale mode can miss its interactions with convectively coupled waves and mesoscale systems, and the Global Data & Global Patterns keynote argued for treating the chain from mesoscale convective systems to the MJO, westerly wind bursts and El Niño as one continuum. Case studies reported propagation regimes influenced by synoptic moist waves and extratropical intrusions, and excessive easterly-wave activity in a forecast model with a biased moisture environment. The final-day discussion proposed multiscale, multi-phenomenon diagnostics. This is a shared framing and a research proposal, not a demonstrated mechanism; the case evidence comes from single events or single models.
insights.reason: The Themes 1+2 keynote was absent from the synthesis, and a framing that recurs in two keynotes, several case studies and the final-day discussion had no insight of its own.

insights.title: Maritime Continent errors persist, and higher resolution alone has not been shown to remove them
insights.text: The prediction keynote reported that MJO events reaching the Maritime Continent weaken or fail to pass in several subseasonal forecast systems, with dry bias, premature weak rainfall, land–sea interactions, topography and the diurnal cycle as candidate causes that were not ranked. The modeling keynote found little support for the expectation that higher horizontal resolution alone improves the MJO, a high-resolution model comparison found mixed effects with propagation biases remaining, and the opening session recommended testing individual deficiencies rather than relying on resolution. Whether AI forecasts show a comparable barrier was left as an empirical question.
insights.reason: Adds the modeling keynote and the opening session, so that modeling lessons are represented.

insights.title: Forecast skill, physical understanding and practical use call for different kinds of validation
insights.text: The closing record named whether improvements in forecast skill also represent improvements in physical understanding as a central question, and treated the two as related but distinct goals. Final-day reports distinguished operational, scientific and model-development uses of AI, and recorded a clear disagreement over whether rigorously validated AI can be trusted without understanding why it succeeds, particularly for extrapolation and extremes. In this reading the objectives are complementary but the evaluation standard is genuinely disputed; neither forecast skill nor feature importance was accepted as evidence of a mechanism.
insights.reason: Aligned with the Q07 reassessment: complementary objectives and a disputed evaluation standard are stated separately.

insights.title: Indices and diagnostics describe complementary aspects of MJO behaviour
insights.text: The closing record kept RMM as a useful common language and recommended supplementing rather than abolishing it. Precipitation-event and object-based analyses reported properties that RMM does not capture in the same way, and the prediction keynote separated circulation-weighted index skill from convection skill. Which supplementary descriptors add value for a specified process or impact target was not settled, and no new index or metric suite was adopted.

insights.title: Improved MJO prediction does not automatically translate into improved regional forecast value
insights.text: The applications keynote noted that gains in MJO index skill need not raise regional impact skill by the same amount, and that MJO-conditioned skill is clearer for tropical rainfall than in the extratropics, where results vary by region, season, metric and study. A case study found very different week-2 extratropical skill among ensembles with similar MJO pattern correlations, and the opening session reported that mid-latitude responses following the MJO remain weaker than observed in recent reforecasts, while recalling a period when better MJO simulation did improve related teleconnection forecasts. Final-day reports traced remote-response errors to heating location, propagation speed and background flow, stressed conditioning on ENSO and season, and stated that better scores are not the same as societal value. No demonstrated decision benefit is recorded.
insights.reason: Supported by the applications keynote, an independent case study, the opening session, regional talks and final-day group reports; Theme 6 had no headline insight before Phase 9.

insights.title: Observational priorities should follow from specific scientific uncertainties, with independent validation data
insights.text: Observers asked theoreticians to specify variables, perturbation scales, sampling intervals and duration before new measurements are designed, and plenary and closing records proposed first cataloguing and reusing existing datasets, some of which remain underused because they are unprocessed. Final-day and observation discussions stressed that reanalysis is not independent observational truth and that AI trained on it may inherit its errors, so independent in situ data are needed for verification. The trade-off between sparse high-precision and denser lower-cost observations, and the priority among core-MJO, remote-impact and process-study observing, remained unresolved.
insights.reason: Adds independence of validation data, which recurs across observation, final-day and AI records.

contested-ai.text: Using validated AI as a practical tool and evaluating it for mechanisms pursue different objectives, and those objectives are complementary. The disagreement recorded in two separate discussion groups concerns the evaluation standard: when validated skill is enough to trust a system beyond its training conditions, and what kind of evidence makes an AI-derived explanation convincing. Whether observations suffice for end-to-end prediction, and whether common or AI-specific metrics should be used, remain open.

themes.title: Global Data & Global Patterns
themes.questions: Is the MJO one expression of tropics-wide and global energy variability? How should precipitation-based measures and long records be used to detect change?

findings.text: Tropical-mean temperature variability under RMM-inactive conditions; interhemispheric energy and mass variations with uncertain transport; increasing precipitation-event measures not seen in RMM; organized convection and momentum transport as neglected processes.

debates.text: Whether RMM inactivity means the absence of MJO-related variability; how sensitive inferred trends are to data period and quality.

unresolved.text: What sets the timescale of the energy oscillation; whether the two energy diagnostics describe one mechanism.

q07.note: The recorded disagreement concerns evaluation standards: when validated forecast skill is enough to trust an AI system beyond its training conditions, and what makes an AI-derived explanation convincing. The underlying objectives—practical forecasting and mechanism identification—are complementary and are not counted as disagreement.
q07.previous: Phase 8: primary C (complementary perspectives), secondary B.

reassessment.text: Retained under Diverging Perspectives. Phase 9 changes the primary relationship from complementary perspectives to different evaluation standards, because two separate discussion groups recorded an explicit, unsettled contrast about what validated skill can justify. The complementary objectives are shown as their own layer, and empirical open questions are separated from positions.

layers.title: Layer 1 · Complementary research objectives
layers.summary: Operational or practical forecasting asks whether a forecast is accurate, reliable and usable; mechanism identification asks which physical processes produce skill and failure. A final-day report listed these as different uses with different requirements.

items.label: Operational or practical forecasting
items.text: Accuracy, reliability and usability for services; users may care more about forecast quality than about the network architecture.

items.label: Physical mechanism identification
items.text: Understanding physical processes and sources of predictability; explaining why forecasts succeed or fail.

layers.title: Layer 2 · Different evaluation standards
layers.summary: The positions conflict where a forecast is used beyond the conditions in which it was validated, and over what counts as understanding.

items.label: When does validated skill support practical use?
items.text: One position holds that rigorous out-of-sample validation justifies use without every user understanding the architecture; the other that outperforming a dynamical model does not show that the right processes were learned, which matters most for extrapolation to new climates and extremes. The closing record framed this as different criteria—out-of-sample skill and practical value versus interpretability, physical consistency and robust generalization—and left it unsettled.

items.label: When is a mechanistic explanation convincing?
items.text: The theory discussion contrasted information-based understanding with the view that AI is a computational procedure that must not be confused with physical explanation, and separated variable importance from causation. The closing discussion answered that explanations must be tested against observations rather than believed.

layers.title: Layer 3 · Open scientific questions
layers.summary: These can be answered by evidence regardless of which evaluation standard one prefers.

items.label: Sufficiency of observational information
items.text: Whether observations alone contain the independent information on winds, humidity and vertical structure that end-to-end prediction of a given target needs.

items.label: Generalization outside the training climate
items.text: Whether skill trained on past data holds for unprecedented climate states and extremes; no validated technique was recorded.

items.label: Physical consistency and interpretability
items.text: Whether an AI model gets the right answer for the right reasons, including conservation and realistic moisture, convection and teleconnections.

items.label: Robustness of AI-derived mechanisms
items.text: Whether a discovered relationship survives equivalent representations, perturbations and held-out regimes; several equations may fit the same trajectories.

evidenceOfDisagreement.text: The final-day record calls the contrast one of the clearest disagreements of the session, its own summary table lists the explainability of AI as an active disagreement, and the closing record states that the discussion did not settle the dispute. Final-day and closing records may overlap and count as one contribution; the theory breakout, plenary and extended minutes form a second, separate discussion group.

distinguishing.text: Layer 2 is not settled by one experiment, but it narrows when claims are bounded: state the lead times, regimes and variables for which skill was validated; test performance on held-out regimes and on climates or extremes outside the training period; attribute skill to resolved modes (for example ENSO or the MJO itself) and to physically admissible perturbations. A forecast that keeps its skill under these tests strengthens the practical-use claim; an explanation that survives them strengthens the mechanistic claim.

reassessment.text: Retained under Diverging Perspectives with the relationship competing hypotheses. Phase 9 restates the competition as one about relative roles, temporal ordering and necessity under specified conditions, not about whether each process exists. The explicit contrast in the records is a single question-and-answer exchange, labelled in the minutes as the discussant's view; observational talks are consistent with several pathways and do not adjudicate among them.

processes.title: Horizontal moisture advection
processes.text: Transport of moisture by anomalous and mean winds, central to advective moisture-mode interpretations of eastward propagation.

processes.title: Moisture convergence
processes.text: Low-level (boundary-layer) convergence that supplies moisture and lifts it; part of multicloud frameworks.

processes.title: Shallow-convective moistening
processes.text: Upward moisture transport by shallow and congestus clouds, observed as stepwise low-to-mid-level moistening and reported to strengthen the MJO in many models.

processes.title: Boundary-layer processes
processes.text: Energy losses to downdrafts and entrainment and their recovery by surface fluxes, which condition when deep convection can develop.

processes.title: Thermodynamic (temperature) contributions to moist static energy
processes.text: Free-tropospheric temperature anomalies that contribute appreciably to MSE during transitions at one site, with seasonal dependence.

q03.interactions: In this editorial framing (not a workshop record), the processes are coupled: convergence drives shallow convection, which redistributes moisture vertically. In a column-integrated budget, shallow-convective moistening is largely an internal redistribution, whereas in a layer budget it is a leading source. Whether the convergence–shallow-convection pathway competes with horizontal advection therefore depends on the budget layer and decomposition, which is why conventions must be fixed before comparing claims.

hypotheses.title: Advection-led
hypotheses.text: During the suppressed-to-active transition east of convection, horizontal moisture advection is the leading term of the column moisture (or MSE) tendency and leads deep-convection onset; removing anomalous horizontal advection in a controlled model slows or removes eastward propagation.

hypotheses.title: Convergence- and shallow-convection-led
hypotheses.text: Low-level convergence and vertical moisture transport by shallow and congestus convection dominate lower-to-mid-tropospheric moistening before deep convection, with moistening appearing first at low levels; suppressing shallow-convective moistening slows propagation even when horizontal advection is retained.

hypotheses.title: Boundary-layer recovery as a gate
hypotheses.text: Recovery of boundary-layer MSE after downdraft and entrainment losses sets when deep convection can develop; this conditions, rather than replaces, H1 or H2.

hypotheses.title: Scope question: temperature contributions
hypotheses.text: If appreciable free-tropospheric temperature contributions during transitions hold beyond one site and season, moisture-only budgets would misattribute part of the MSE tendency. Whether temperature anomalies are a driver, a response or a covarying component is open.

conditions.text: The hypotheses need not have the same answer everywhere: the records already show seasonal dependence at one site (boreal winter versus spring), and the relative weights may change between the Indian Ocean, the Maritime Continent and the western Pacific and between events.

tests.title: Layer-resolved budgets with frozen conventions
tests.text: Compute boundary-layer, lower- and upper-tropospheric moisture and MSE budgets around transition onset, with closure residuals, and compare the lead times of advection, convergence and vertical-transport terms (H1 versus H2 ordering).

tests.title: Column versus layer budgets
tests.text: H2 predicts large vertical redistribution with a small net column source from shallow convection; H1 predicts a column tendency dominated by horizontal advection.

tests.title: Mechanism-denial experiments across a model hierarchy
tests.text: Separately remove anomalous horizontal moisture advection, suppress shallow-convective moisture transport, and alter boundary-layer downdraft or surface-flux effects, diagnosing induced mean-state change in each case.

tests.title: Independent multi-site soundings
tests.text: Test temperature versus moisture contributions by layer and season at several sites, using soundings that were not assimilated into the reanalysis being compared.

numericalUncertainty.text: Percentages of temperature and moisture contributions at Manus remain withheld: the reported shares do not add up to the whole, so their denominator is unresolved. Ratios of downdraft and entrainment contributions and boundary-layer flux estimates come from automatic transcripts and single campaigns and are not reproduced here. Event samples per season are small.

evidenceState.text: One recorded exchange contrasts H1 and H2; observations and models reported at the workshop are consistent with several pathways; no recorded analysis discriminated among them.

problem.text: RMM limitations for convection, regional rainfall and structure are noted in independent talks and in the closing record.

method.text: Supplement RMM rather than replace it: recommended in the closing record and echoed by the prediction keynote and event-based talks.

physics.text: The question concerns diagnostics, not a physical explanation.

endorsement.text: No index, metric suite or performance threshold was adopted.

remaining.text: Which descriptors add value for which target; simplicity versus richer structure; what each descriptor would know at forecast time.

problem.text: Evaluation designs make reported skill incomparable; rapidly updated AI versions strain reforecast-based comparison; skill and predictability estimate different quantities.

method.text: Common, reproducible benchmarks and real-time comparison as a complement to reforecasts were proposed, but whether AI needs its own metrics remained disputed.

physics.text: No shared explanation of why particular systems gain skill.

endorsement.text: No benchmark specification was approved, and no agreement to abandon reforecasts was reached.

remaining.text: Metric choice, sample adequacy for rare regimes, freezing versions, availability of process outputs.

problem.text: Index skill is not regional value: stated in the applications keynote, a case study, the prediction Q&A, the closing record and final-day reports.

method.text: Conditional, regional evaluation against simple baselines and with ENSO and season, and co-design with users. The final-day minutes label regional impact evaluation and co-design as broad convergence; that is the minutes' characterization, not a resolution.

physics.text: A shared framework of teleconnection error sources (heating location, propagation speed, background flow) was reported, but not an agreed explanation of why remote responses are too weak.

endorsement.text: Volunteers came forward for practical activities at the close, but no adopted plan with owners, deadlines or deliverables is recorded.

remaining.text: Incremental skill after conditioning; which targets matter to which users; whether any realized benefit exists.

disagreement_matrix.question: What evidence establishes an MJO mechanism?

a.text: Diagnostics that separate better- from worse-performing models carry evidence about mechanisms.

b.text: Mechanism claims require tests of a theory's assumptions: process interventions in independent models and falsifying observations.

disagreement_matrix.compatible: Partly: as successive steps they combine; they conflict only if diagnostic skill alone is taken to identify the mechanism in nature.

distinguish.text: Matched process-suppression experiments in independent models; per-theory lists of observations that would contradict it.

uncertainty.text: Tuning, compensating errors and induced mean-state change confound interventions.

disagreement_matrix.evidence: Recorded in one discussion group (breakout, plenary and extended minutes); no test performed.

disagreement_matrix.question: Which pathway leads moistening before deep convection?

a.text: Horizontal moisture advection leads the column moisture tendency.

b.text: Low-level convergence and shallow-convective moistening lead lower-to-mid-tropospheric moistening.

disagreement_matrix.compatible: Not mutually exclusive; they compete over dominance, ordering and necessity under specified conditions and budget conventions.

distinguish.text: Layer-resolved budgets with frozen conventions and lead–lag analysis; mechanism-denial experiments.

uncertainty.text: Single-site and cruise sampling, budget residuals, assimilation dependence, ASR-derived numbers.

disagreement_matrix.evidence: One recorded exchange; observations consistent with several pathways.

disagreement_matrix.question: How does the stratosphere modulate MJO convection?

a.text: Stratospheric winds alter the vertical tilt and phase of an ice-cloud radiative feedback.

b.text: Organized mesoscale convection is a common missing process linking QBO coupling and the Maritime Continent barrier.

disagreement_matrix.compatible: Could interact; unequal evidence (an idealized model result versus an untested proposal).

distinguish.text: Factorial experiments varying stratospheric winds, cloud-radiative coupling and organized-convection treatment.

uncertainty.text: Simplified model physics; model-dependent significance; ENSO and seasonal confounding.

disagreement_matrix.evidence: Two separate talks' records; neither tested the other pathway.

disagreement_matrix.question: What can validated AI skill justify?

a.text: Rigorous out-of-sample validation justifies bounded practical use without full understanding of the architecture.

b.text: Skill does not show that the right processes were learned; trust beyond validated conditions requires mechanistic understanding.

disagreement_matrix.compatible: The objectives are compatible; the standards conflict where use extends beyond validated conditions.

distinguish.text: Held-out regimes and out-of-distribution climates; attribution of skill to resolved modes; physically admissible perturbations.

uncertainty.text: Training overlap, black-box access, correlated inputs.

disagreement_matrix.evidence: Explicit and unsettled in two separate discussion groups.

disagreement_matrix.question: Should AI and dynamical forecasts be judged by the same metrics?

a.text: The same physical and forecast metrics should apply wherever possible, for comparability.

b.text: AI systems need fundamentally new or AI-specific diagnostics for their distinctive failure modes.

disagreement_matrix.compatible: Largely: a common core plus AI-specific diagnostics; the dispute is over sufficiency of the common core.

distinguish.text: Whether AI-specific diagnostics detect failures that common metrics miss on matched cases.

uncertainty.text: Restricted AI output variables limit common process diagnostics.

disagreement_matrix.question: Why do forecasts weaken or stall the MJO over the Maritime Continent?

a.text: Local moisture, diurnal-cycle and land–sea processes (dry bias, premature weak rain).

b.text: Background SST and interacting disturbances control propagation regimes, so local convection alone is incomplete.

disagreement_matrix.compatible: Not exclusive and not ranked; both may act in different events.

distinguish.text: Matched crossing versus stalled events; tendency comparisons; controlled SST and convection experiments.

uncertainty.text: Case-specific experiments; mixed resolutions and periods.

disagreement_matrix.evidence: Candidate causes listed in a keynote and case studies; not ranked.

complementary.title: RMM and supplementary diagnostics
complementary.text: A compact common index and richer convective, event-based or regional descriptors answer different questions.

complementary.title: Reforecasts and real-time comparison
complementary.text: Large conditional samples versus evaluation of current model versions.

complementary.title: Precision and coverage of observations
complementary.text: A target-dependent design trade-off, not a contest of observing strategies.

complementary.title: Regional contributions
complementary.text: Different regions, hazards and users; none opposes using MJO information.

complementary.title: Levels of lifecycle explanation
complementary.text: Background conditions, finite-amplitude growth and multiscale development as potentially complementary levels.

complementary.title: Practical forecasting and mechanism identification
complementary.text: Different uses of AI with different requirements (Layer 1 of the Q07 analysis).

complementary.title: Simple and comprehensive models
complementary.text: Contrasting viewpoints on simple versus fully coupled high-resolution models were recorded, but both fit within a model hierarchy; no community initiative was agreed.

dependencies.reason: Crossing, stalled and terminated events must be defined before passage errors can be compared across systems.
Versioned, reviewed index implementations must exist before differences in forecast skill can be interpreted.
Training and assimilation lineage of verification data must be known before skill on held-out cases is credited as generalization.
Independent observations are needed before an AI explanation is judged to generalize beyond its training data.
The practical-use position depends on matched, validated skill; explanations of skill presuppose that the skill is real.
AI and dynamical passage errors can be compared only on matched cases with comparable information.
Process budgets are needed before an improvement in passage is attributed to a propagation mechanism.
Transition-phase budgets need a transition definition; existing phase definitions allow a provisional start.
Theory comparisons need the MJO behaviour each theory claims to explain to be specified.
Phase-resolved budgets are among the observables for discriminating mechanism claims.
Budgets validated against assimilated soundings are not independent; the lineage register identifies independent data.
Index-based and precipitation-based passage can disagree; versioned diagnostics make that visible.
Added MJO descriptors are judged against regional targets.
Trend definitions depend on how events and indices are defined.
Observing-system changes must be recorded before trends are interpreted.

action-q11: A clearly defined hazard or decision target, specified with users
action-q08: Access to reforecast archives and AI forecasts with documented versions and training cutoffs
action-q09: Model tendency or budget outputs where mechanism claims are made
action-q07: Access to AI model inputs and outputs sufficient for perturbation tests
action-q05: A model in which cloud-radiative coupling and convection treatment can be varied
action-q01: At least one simple and one comprehensive model suitable for process-suppression experiments
action-q12: Multiple precipitation products over a common period

pilots.title: Maritime Continent MJO Prediction Barrier
pilots.objective: Identify systematic differences in MJO propagation and passage errors over the Maritime Continent among AI and dynamical forecast systems.
pilots.status: The existence of a barrier in AI forecasts, and any dependence of the barrier on season, background state or convective latitude, are open questions in the records. This pilot tests them; it does not assume them.

hypotheses.text: Systems that weaken or stall MJO events over the Maritime Continent show a dry lower-tropospheric bias and premature light rainfall ahead of convection relative to independent observations, and systems or events without these biases pass more often.
If passage errors depend on season, ENSO state or the latitude of convection, error rates stratified by these factors differ by more than event-block sampling uncertainty.
Null hypothesis: AI and dynamical systems have indistinguishable passage-failure rates on matched events. Rejection in either direction informs whether the barrier is a parameterization artefact.
An apparent improvement in index-based passage persists in precipitation and in independent regional observations.

dimensions: Diurnal convection over land and sea
data: An observed reference from more than one product for OLR, precipitation, winds and humidity, with each product's assimilation lineage recorded
Reforecasts from at least two dynamical subseasonal systems over a common period
At least one AI forecast system with a documented training cutoff and the output variables needed (precipitation or humidity, not only index components)
Independent in situ or radar data over the Maritime Continent where available
tools: Versioned RMM and OLR-based index code
An event tracker with reviewed onset, crossing, stalling and termination criteria
Event- or year-block resampling for uncertainty
Provenance logging of every dataset version
pilots.classification: Events are identified first in observations at verification time (crossing, stalled, terminated, jumping), then matched by initialization date in each system. Every threshold is varied over a predeclared range, and results are reported for each setting.
metrics: Latitude error of the convective centre
Precipitation and column-moisture bias in the week before arrival
Diurnal-cycle amplitude and phase over land and sea
Index-based and field-based scores reported side by side
pilots.uncertainty: Resample by event or year, not by day; report sample counts per stratum; report the spread among reference products; treat strata with too few events as inconclusive.
pilots.mve: One dynamical and one AI system, one boreal-winter common period, index- and precipitation-based passage only, with threshold sensitivity.
criteria: A passage-error difference counts only if it exceeds event-block uncertainty under all predeclared thresholds.
A claimed improvement must persist in precipitation and in at least one independent reference.
Mechanistic interpretation is withheld unless process budgets are available (see dependencies).
outputs: Observed Maritime Continent passage catalogue with labels and threshold sensitivity
Error-decomposition tables by system, lead time and stratum
An output-availability audit for AI systems
A specification for a small controlled experiment, if the results justify one
risks: AI systems without precipitation or humidity outputs
Overlap between training and evaluation periods
Reanalysis dependence of the reference over the Maritime Continent
roles: Verification analyst independent of model development
Liaison with AI developers on outputs and training periods

pilots.title: MJO Index Disagreement Catalogue
pilots.objective: Determine when RMM, OMI, ROMI and event-based diagnostics give substantially different characterizations of MJO behaviour.
pilots.status: The records show that diagnostics answer different questions and can disagree; they do not show where or how often. This pilot measures that.

hypotheses.text: Disagreement in phase or amplitude classification beyond a prespecified tolerance is concentrated in identifiable conditions—season, convection displaced from the equator, weak or noncanonical events—rather than spread uniformly.
Real-time indices differ from retrospective OMI most near event onset and termination, because of endpoint treatment.
Disagreement cases have physically distinct full-field structures (for example strong circulation with weak convection) and are not merely index noise.
Inferred trends in event frequency depend on the descriptor; the sign or magnitude differs between precipitation-event and index-based definitions over a common period.

protocol.title: Common evaluation periods
protocol.text: Use one common period with identical missing-data masks for all diagnostics.

protocol.title: Versioned index definitions
protocol.text: Record provider, version and retrieval date for each series; treat differently named products as different indices.

protocol.title: Filtering and phase conventions
protocol.text: Document filters, EOF bases and climatologies; align OMI and RMM phase conventions once and check whether a supplied product is already aligned.

protocol.title: Real-time versus retrospective information
protocol.text: Register what each index could know at issue time and keep retrospective series out of forecast inputs.

protocol.title: Event identification
protocol.text: Define events by amplitude threshold and duration and, separately, by object tracking, with predeclared settings.

protocol.title: Seasonal dependence
protocol.text: Stratify by season, including boreal summer.

protocol.title: Regional differences
protocol.text: Compare classifications against regional rainfall and convection fields.

protocol.title: Noncanonical events
protocol.text: Label stalling, jumping, slow and fast events explicitly rather than removing them.

data: Published RMM, OMI and ROMI series with version documentation
OLR and precipitation fields over the same period
tools: Index computation or retrieval scripts with checksums of retrieved files
An object tracker for event-based diagnostics
pilots.classification: For each day and each pair of diagnostics, record agreement in phase (within a tolerance), amplitude class and event membership; classify disagreement cases by their full-field structure.
metrics: Phase agreement rate and circular phase difference
Event-level onset and termination timing differences
Contingency tables by season and region
pilots.uncertainty: Year-block resampling; sensitivity to tolerance and thresholds; repeat with alternative product versions.
pilots.mve: RMM and ROMI over one common period, daily phase and amplitude agreement by season, with a list of disagreement cases.
criteria: Hypotheses are tested against predeclared tolerances, not chosen after inspection.
A disagreement class counts as physical only if its full-field composite differs beyond resampling uncertainty.
Agreement between indices is not treated as validation of either.
outputs: A reproducible catalogue of dates, diagnostics and disagreement classes
A disagreement atlas of full-field composites
A metric card for each diagnostic
risks: Licensing or redistribution limits on series
Silent version changes in published products
Circularity when event definitions use one of the compared indices
roles: Maintainers of index products (for version documentation)

d30: Write the phase-convention crosswalk and tolerances
Retrieve series and record checksums and retrieval dates
d60: Compute daily agreement statistics over the common period
Identify and stratify disagreement cases by season and region
d90: Composite full fields for disagreement classes
Add object-based events and the real-time versus retrospective comparison
Release a draft catalogue for review

pilots.title: Observational Requirements & Data Rescue
pilots.objective: Determine which existing observations and which additional measurements would most effectively reduce uncertainty in specific MJO processes.
pilots.status: The records ask for observing requirements tied to scientific questions and for reuse of existing data; they do not identify which gaps matter most. This pilot proposes a question-driven gap analysis.

hypotheses.text: For transition-phase moisture budgets, existing quality-controlled sounding and ship data can constrain the sign and ordering of leading terms; adding sites reduces uncertainty in the seasonal dependence more than adding precision at one site.

A substantial fraction of nominally available validation observations over the Maritime Continent has entered reanalysis assimilation or AI training, so genuinely independent verification sets are smaller than inventories suggest.
For a selected target, subsampling and controlled-noise experiments identify whether coverage or precision limits uncertainty.

components.title: Existing data inventory
components.text: Datasets, variables, coordinates, cadence, custodians, access routes and usage terms, including campaign data that are unprocessed or hard to find.

components.title: Measurement uncertainty
components.text: Documented accuracy and known biases for each instrument type.

components.title: Spatial and temporal sampling
components.text: Station density, revisit and averaging intervals relative to the process timescale.

components.title: Vertical information requirements
components.text: Profiles of winds, humidity and temperature that budgets and end-to-end AI questions require.

components.title: Boundary-layer and air–sea observations
components.text: Surface fluxes, boundary-layer MSE, downdraft and entrainment diagnostics.

components.title: Data availability and quality
components.text: Quality flags, gaps and processing needs.

components.title: Independence from assimilation and AI training
components.text: A lineage flag for each dataset and period.

components.title: Reanalysis validation
components.text: Which reanalysis quantities can be checked against data that were not assimilated.

data: Metadata from existing field campaigns and long-term sites (for example DYNAMO ship data and long-term soundings at Manus)
tools: Subsampling and noise-injection scripts for a chosen diagnostic
pilots.classification: Start from two or three process uncertainties chosen with researchers (for example the Q03 transition budget and Maritime Continent diurnal convection); for each, list required variables, resolution, duration and independence, then map existing data against them.
metrics: Coverage of each requirement by existing data
Fraction of candidate validation data independent of assimilation and training
Uncertainty in the chosen diagnostic as a function of sites, sampling and noise
pilots.uncertainty: Subsampling experiments inherit the error of the reference; report the reference's limitations; mark unknown lineage explicitly.
pilots.mve: One process target, a requirement matrix and an inventory of known datasets with lineage flags.
criteria: A sampling strategy is judged useful only if it reduces uncertainty in the chosen diagnostic, or improves held-out verification, under matched resources.
No generic claim that more sensors or more precision is always better.
No procurement or data redistribution is implied.
outputs: A requirement matrix (process → variable → resolution → duration → existing source → independence → gap)
Sensitivity curves of uncertainty versus coverage and precision
risks: Subsampling studies inherit model or reference error
Effort to process legacy data underestimated
roles: Process scientists who define the targets

collaboration.text: Needs several forecast systems and regional observations.

roadmap.status: Three candidate pilot projects proposed in this personal report. They are editorial proposals, not workshop priorities, and no one has been asked or assigned to carry them out. Planning horizons are not promised completion dates.

plenary-themes-3-4.text: The theory plenary contrasted moisture-mode diagnostics that discriminate model performance with tests that manipulate the processes a theory requires, and debated information-based understanding of AI and the use of physics constraints.

daehyun-kim-modeling.text: Reviewed how MJO simulation has progressed: the expectation that higher horizontal resolution alone improves the MJO has found little support, whereas moisture-sensitive convection, shallow-convective moistening, the mean state and vertical structure have been implicated more consistently; process-level explanation remains needed.

stephanie-rushley-north-pacific-cyclones.text: Found very different week-2 extratropical geopotential-height skill among ensembles with similar MJO pattern correlations in a high-wave case, and distinguished humidity errors from displacement of the forecast MJO in space and time.

daisuke-takasuka-deterministic-chaotic.text: In NICAM ensemble case studies, one of two cases branched into fast and slow propagation regimes; replacing its sea-surface temperatures with those of the other case removed the branching, which the speaker interpreted as control by equatorial SST symmetry.

breakout-themes-3-4.text: The breakout record asked for objective criteria to tell weakening, stalled propagation and termination of MJO events apart, separated variable importance from causation, and proposed testing equation discovery first on systems whose equations are already known.

qoosaku-moteki-cens-mjo.text: The site author's own talk record notes that the question-and-answer exchange left the proposed feedback of cross-equatorial northerly surges onto the MJO, and the associated pressure-system dynamics, untested.

kenedy-silverio-southern-africa.text: Reported MJO-related summer rainfall anomalies over southern Africa whose amplitude and location varied with ENSO while the basic pattern was largely shared (programme topic: ENSO-dependent impacts on southern African summer rainfall).

mitch-moncrieff-global-data-global-patte.text: Argued that convective parameterizations have neglected the momentum transport and dynamical organization of mesoscale convective systems, and recommended evaluating organized convection against Maritime Continent passage, tropical spectra, El Niño onset and QBO relations rather than MJO amplitude alone.

mapping_review.finding: The automatic transcript of the full recording in this programme slot opens with the speaker introducing the talk as published work on detecting the MJO robustly from limited data, motivated by short kilometre-scale simulations. The minutes therefore appear to belong to this talk, and the difference from the programme title reflects the talk's content rather than misfiled minutes.

Its later plenary-debate section could belong to either session.
